Dear Parents, Residents, and Community Partners,

The School Board’s FY27 Adopted Budget is centered on investing both today and in the future, aligning
with the One LCPS 2027 Strategic Plan for Excellence. The adopted FY27 School Operating Fund budget
totals $2,066,954,668 and supports 13,570.1 full-time positions. This reflects an increase of $104,809,886,
or 5.3 percent, including a projected $105,000,000 increase in local funding from Loudoun County offset by
a marginal net decrease in other funding streams.

State funding is projected to decline by $3,342,774 based on the Governor’s proposed 2026-2028
Biennium Budget. It is important to note that the Governor’s proposals must still be considered and adopted
by the Virginia General Assembly, which may make changes during their deliberations through the spring of
2026. Changes in state revenue projections will be brought to the School Board for consideration.

The FY27 Adopted Budget reflects changes across several key funds. The Grant Fund increases by $1.6
million, primarily due to anticipated growth in federal grant funding for the division. The School Nutrition
Fund increases by $1.2 million based on salary and benefit cost increase as well as inflationary pressures
on food and materials. Lastly, the Self Insurance Fund grows by $71.1 million, largely due to higher
utilization and rapidly rising medical costs, particularly for prescription drugs.

The Capital Improvement Projects (CIP) Fund and the Capital Asset Preservation Program (CAPP) Fund
are described in greater detail in the School Board’s adopted FY27–32 CIP and CAPP budgets.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

As we have often noted, Loudoun County benefits from the shared commitment of the School Board, the
Board of Supervisors and our community to sustain a strong public education system. Our school
community holds high expectations for educational excellence across a wide range of learning pathways,
supported by comprehensive services designed to meet the needs of every student.

The estimated local tax transfer reflects a year-over-year increase of $105 million, consistent with the
County’s budget guidance and mindful of the more limited fiscal conditions under which the County is
operating. This Adopted Budget is both fiscally aligned and intentionally focused on the theme of continuing
to invest today and in the future, while fulfilling the requirements of the Code of Virginia to estimate the
funding necessary to support our public schools.

As noted earlier, the Governor’s proposed budget results in a projected decline in state funding. While it
does include additional funding from basic aid and state sales taxes for the first year of the biennium, these
increases are more than offset by reductions due to lower enrollment, the shift from a 3% pay increase this
year to 2% next year, and other rebenchmarking adjustments, such as changes to the local composite
index that shift a larger share of funding responsibility from the state to the county.

As the general assembly now works on the budget, the school division will continue to monitor the state
budget and its impact on LCPS.

Virginia has a constitutional responsibility to fund public education; however, a 2023 Joint Legislative Audit
and Review Commission (JLARC) report highlights that the state’s per-student funding for K–12 education
remains below the national average, the regional average, and the funding levels of three of Virginia’s five
neighboring states. While investments in education continue to grow, these gaps mean that LCPS receives
significantly less per student compared with many other states, resulting in substantial lost funding each
year.

We appreciate the General Assembly’s ongoing attention to the JLARC findings and have outlined the
continuation of the JLARC study on education funding as a priority in our legislative program. Despite gaps
in state funding, LCPS remains focused on its key priorities: supporting employee compensation and
expanding opportunities for students. These investments align with the ONE LCPS Strategic Plan and
reflect the School Board’s discussions during budget workshops about what matters most to the division
and the communities we serve.

Enrollment is a critical factor in budget planning, and LCPS is entering a period of declining enrollment. For
FY27, enrollment is projected at 316 students fewer than this year’s actual count, and CIP projections
indicate continued declines each year through FY32. This trend underscores the importance of careful
planning to ensure resources are aligned with student needs.

A frequent question is why the school budget continues to increase when student enrollment has slowed.
As a reminder, about 90% of the increase in expenditures for FY27 are in personnel costs. As an example,
for LCPS, providing a basic annual step increase alone costs roughly $29 million. If employees then receive
cost of living adjustments, our operating budget will increase, even with no new positions. In addition, there
are typically increases in benefits costs as healthcare becomes more expensive, and there are other fixed
costs that grow despite level or declining enrollment – things like fuel and utility costs that we do not
control. This concept is important to understand as it directly relates to LCPS for FY27.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

With this context in mind, the Adopted Budget for the 2026–2027 school year reflects thoughtful
investments that strengthen our schools today while preparing for the future.

Investing in our Empowered Students

The needs of our students continue to evolve, and while division wide enrollment is declining, the number
of students requiring more resources continues to increase. For example, our English Learner population is
projected to increase by 1.0% and our special education population by 3.4%. As a result, 50.6 additional
teachers, teacher assistants, and other positions providing these specialized supports for students and
specialized programs are included.

Of the total 13,570.1 positions in the school operating fund, 94.2% are working in the schools or directly
with staff and students. These FTEs may be school-based or school-facing. School-facing positions are the
employees who may not be assigned to a school, but routinely work in our schools. This Adopted Budget
keeps additional staffing resources focused on students.

Expanded Academic Offerings and Access

The FY27 Adopted Budget prioritizes providing students with expanded academic opportunities and robust
support to help them thrive. Expanded academic offerings and access include additional teachers and
instructional coaches across grade levels, as well as continued support for Board-approved, specialized
programs such as the Elementary Dual-Language Immersion program, the Academy of Global and
Linguistic Studies, Career IB Program, and enhanced resources for the R.I.S.E. Academy. Students also
benefit from new athletic programs, a new JROTC program, and more equitable access to fine arts and
CTE courses through course fee eliminations.

Additional Student Supports

Student support is strengthened through targeted investments in mental and behavioral health services,
threat assessment coordination, additional resources for English Language Learners and Special
Education, and specialized support within the R.I.S.E. Academy. These investments ensure LCPS
continues to provide all students with the opportunities and resources they need to succeed.

Additionally, meal prices will remain unchanged for next year after a series of meal price increases. To
support the school nutrition fund, a transfer from the School Operating Fund is budgeted to help cover
operational costs.

Investing in our Exemplary Staff

The One LCPS Strategic Plan identifies teachers, administrators, and staff as the most important
contributors to student success in our schools, second only to families. This Adopted Budget reflects that
priority through meaningful investments in employee salaries and benefits, consistent with the first LCPS
collective bargaining agreement.

The operating budget provides the resources necessary to support the day-to-day operations of the school
division while offering competitive salary and benefits packages for employees. Maintaining competitive
compensation is essential to recruiting, retaining, and supporting a highly qualified and dedicated

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

workforce. The collective bargaining agreement includes provisions for an annual step increase and top-of-
scale payment, as well as a cost-of-living adjustment ranging from 4% to 5% depending on the employee
group.

As health care costs continue to increase, the FY27 Adopted Budget also includes measures to strengthen
the financial stability of the health self-insurance fund. These efforts combine cost-containment strategies
with revenue enhancements, including a 20% increase in health insurance premiums shared by both
employees and the employer.

Investing in our Enriched School System

The FY27 Adopted Budget includes focused investments to support the safe, efficient, and effective
operation of our schools. These investments address division-wide needs while accounting for inflationary
cost pressures.

Key priorities include enhancements to security staffing and technology, continued implementation of the
new ERP system, and operational staffing needed to maintain continuity of services across schools and
support departments. Together, these investments reinforce LCPS’s commitment to safe, well-supported
learning environments for students and staff.

Investing in our Engaged Community

The FY27 Adopted Budget includes investments that enhance communication, outreach, and engagement
with families and the community. These resources support expanded language access, additional family
liaison services, and tools to better connect with families. By strengthening partnerships between schools
and the families they serve, these investments help ensure all students have the support they need while
reinforcing LCPS’s commitment to both responsive and proactive community engagement.

Delayed Investments

The FY27 Adopted Budget was developed to balance critical needs with projected resources, rather than
as a full needs-based budget. As a result, some important priorities from Board members, staff, and other
stakeholders cannot be fully funded this year. These items, which have previously been referred to as
“unmet needs,” can also be thought of as delayed investments – important initiatives that will be
considered.
Examples of delayed investments include:
 • Slower expansion of programs and initiatives
 • Additional positions and staffing enhancements across departments to support students and staff
 • Employee tuition assistance programs
 • Delayed start of new programs
 • Phased-in approach to remodeling the stipend framework across the division

Despite the funding obstacles outlined earlier, LCPS continues to thrive.
Here are just a few of many LCPS accomplishments over the last year:

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 • The LCPS Class of 2025 graduated 6,932 seniors, with nearly 75% receiving an advanced
 diploma, almost 24% a standard diploma, and just over 1% an applied studies diploma. Almost
 70% of graduates reported they will attend a four-year college, while over 17% will attend a two-
 year school, and 2% will enter military service. LCPS has a 97.2% on-time graduation rate.
 • National Merit Scholarship winners included 18 LCPS students for the 2024-2025 school year. Five
 students won college-sponsored scholarships, eleven were named National Merit $2,500
 Scholarship winners, and two received corporate-sponsored National Merit Scholarships.
 • Niche’s Virginia rankings placed LCPS as the 4th Best School District and the 2nd Best School
 District for Athletes. Seven high schools are listed in the top 20 in the state, with Independence
 High School ranked as the #2 high school in Virginia.
 • In collaboration with George Mason University and NOVA, LCPS launched the ACCESS Academy
 at Potomac Falls High School to provide dual-enrollment credits, IT certifications and real-world
 learning for students pursuing high-demand tech careers.
 • LCPS expanded programming options that care for students’ well-being and academic needs. For
 example, LCPS will support students in early recovery from substance use disorders with a
 recovery academy offering academic and therapeutic support.
 • The division continues its focus on workforce development and future-ready education, focusing on
 key industries like cybersecurity, health innovation, and aerospace. LCPS also hosted a Workforce
 Summit, bringing together more than 250 community and business leaders.
 • In partnership with the Loudoun Education Foundation and Amazon, LCPS launched four new
 Think Big Corners at elementary schools, bringing hands-on STEM learning directly to students.
 • The Family and Community Engagement Office launched the LCPS Family Academy - a series of
 free virtual workshops to help families support academic success, understand school
 communications, and avoid the “summer melt.”
 • The division also hosted its first series of Student Success Talks in each district across the county,
 connecting families with LCPS leadership and providing tools for academic, social, and emotional
 student success.
 • Watson Mountain Middle School opened its doors, becoming LCPS’ 100th school, and honored its
 historical roots with a dedication ceremony that celebrated the legacy of the land and the
 community’s future.
 • To further open communication, the division developed a monthly video series called Think Fast,
 and launched the LCPS podcast. Both highlight stories and voices from across the division on
 education trends, programs, and student success.
 • The ONE LCPS Celebration Day had schools and staff across the division celebrating community,
 culture, and collaboration with a day of fun-filled events and friendly competitions to honor the
 LCPS spirit.

 Loudoun County Public Schools
 Organization

 Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS) is organized to focus on empowering all 80,201 students to
 make meaningful contributions to the world, while managing 98 schools, five non-comprehensive schools
 and 15 support buildings. It is a rapidly growing, dynamic, well-managed and efficient organization.

 Nine elected School Board members govern LCPS. The members are elected to four-year terms. One
 member represents each of the County’s eight magisterial districts and there is one at-large member. The
 School Board is charged by Virginia law and the regulations of the Virginia Board of Education to establish
 policies, guidelines, and rules that will ensure the proper administration of the County’s school programs.

 The Superintendent works closely with twelve members of Cabinet to oversee the day-to-day operations of
 the schools and support services.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 Overview and LCPS Accomplishments
Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS) is led by Superintendent Dr. Aaron Spence, who conducted the
first-ever LCPS Student Success talks, connecting families with LCPS leadership, providing tools for
academic, social and emotional student success, and belonging.

In the 2024-2025 school year, more than 80,000 students were enrolled across 98 schools and five non-
comprehensive schools in LCPS, and the division employed over 13,000 staff. The division’s workplace
excellence is recognized by Forbes’ list of America’s Best-in-State Employers, 2024.

The Washington Post 2025 area awards went to Principal of the Year, Jeff Joseph of Dominion Trail
Elementary and Teacher of the Year, Kimberly Poole, at J. Lupton Simpson Middle School.

Students Are Front and Center
The LCPS Class of 2025 graduated 6,932 seniors, with nearly 75% receiving an advanced diploma, almost
24% a standard diploma, and just over 1% an applied studies diploma. Almost 70% of graduates reported
they will attend a four-year college, while over 17% will attend a two-year school, and 2% will enter military
service. LCPS has a 97.2% on-time graduation rate.

National Merit Scholarship winners included 18 LCPS students for the 2024-2025 school year. Five
students won college-sponsored scholarships, eleven were named National Merit $2,500 Scholarship
winners, and two received corporate-sponsored National Merit Scholarships.

Niche’s Virginia rankings placed LCPS as the 4th Best School District and the 2nd Best School District for
Athletes. Seven high schools are listed in the top 20 in the state, with Independence High School ranked as
the #2 best high school in Virginia.

In August, the Virginia Department of Education (VDOE) released the 2025 Standards of Learning (SOL)
test results, which showed that for LCPS, SOL proficiency rates have increased or stayed the same in all
subject areas. LCPS significantly outpaced Virginia in all five subject areas: English Reading; English
Writing; History and Social Sciences; Mathematics and Science.

School and Community Programming
In collaboration with George Mason University and NOVA, LCPS launched the ACCESS Academy at
Potomac Falls High School to provide dual-enrollment credits, IT certifications and real-world learning for
students pursuing high-demand tech careers.

LCPS expanded programming options that care for students’ well-being and academic needs. LCPS will
support students in early recovery from substance use disorders with a recovery academy offering
academic and therapeutic support. Planning is also underway for the Academy of Global and Linguistic
Studies, a future-forward program with pathways in Global Leadership and Global Business featuring
immersive Arabic and Mandarin instruction.

The division continues its focus on workforce development and future-ready education, focusing on key
industries like cybersecurity, health innovation, and aerospace, by hosting the first LCPS Workforce
Summit, bringing together more than 250 community and business leaders.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

In partnership with the Loudoun Education Foundation and Amazon, LCPS launched four new Think Big
Corners at elementary schools, bringing hands-on STEM learning directly to students.
Now in its third year, the LCPS Dual Language Immersion program for elementary students starts students
off early on a successful path through daily, immersive instruction in English and Spanish. Elementary
students build foundational literacy, numeracy and collaboration skills in two languages while embracing
the rich diversity of their classrooms.

Engaging with Families
The Division of Family and Community Engagement launched the
LCPS Family Academy – a series of free virtual workshops to
help families support their students’ academic success and
navigate and access school division resources empowering
families to be partners in their child’s education.

The results from the Annual Family Survey, 2025, reveal what
happens when LCPS leads with listening, engagement and
belonging:
 - More families reported feeling empowered to be partners
 in their child’s education.
 - Families said LCPS is doing a better job of
 communicating - especially around clubs, activities and
 teacher expectations.
 - High school parents reported increased confidence that
 we’re preparing their children for life after graduation.
 - And most importantly, LCPS saw an increase in families
 who said their schools feel welcoming, inclusive and
 respectful of diversity.

Operational Excellence
The FY26 budget focused on three priorities: placing students at
the center of our work, recruiting and retaining the best and the brightest, and supporting new and ongoing
initiatives. Fully 94.2% of the FTEs in the FY26 budget are school-based and school-facing employees.
LCPS has an average cost per pupil of $23,825.

For the past five years, LCPS has provided educators with funds to set up their classrooms, with first-year
teachers eligible for a classroom supply allotment of $250 and returning teachers eligible to receive a $100
allotment for supplies.

LCPS has more than 750 buses covering over 500 routes to and from the division’s 100 school buildings,
logging approximately eight million miles annually to transport students.

LCPS has implemented its first Sustainability Framework, formalizing the division’s commitment to
environmental responsibility by integrating sustainability into instruction, operations, leadership and long-
term planning.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 FY27 Budget Preparation Process

The Code of Virginia requires that the Division Superintendent submit to the governing body, with the
approval of the School Board, an estimate of the funds needed during the next fiscal year for support of the
public schools. In Virginia, school divisions are fiscally dependent on the local governing body, which for
Loudoun, is the County Board of Supervisors.

The following calendar of events more fully explains the activities that contributed to the budget development
and approval process this year:

May – June
 • LCPS staff request funding for programs, maintaining facilities and major building improvements.
 • Budget Priorities work session with the School Board.

August – September
 • Budget instructions are distributed by the Budget and Financial Analytics Division to the Departments
 to provide guidance for the development of future year budget requests.
 • Preliminary staffing standard reviews are held with departments.
 • Host budget exercises to solicit input for FY27 investments and priorities.

October – December
 • Revised revenue update provided to the School Board.
 • Budget requests are received by Budget and Financial Analytics for review and analysis.
 • The staffing as of September 30 is analyzed and current year costs for salaries and benefits are
 used for estimating the future year compensation costs. Salary and benefits represent
 approximately 90% of the operating budget.
 • Staffing standard meetings with departments to finalize staffing for the upcoming year.
 • Estimated federal, state and local revenue is developed.
 • The Superintendent meets with department and division budget holders to review and modify
 budget requests.
 • Conduct a second budget work session with the School Board to identify priorities and receive
 early budget guidance.
 • The results of these meetings are analyzed and compiled by the Budget and Financial Analytics
 Division and a draft budget document is prepared for review by the Superintendent and Cabinet.
 • Preliminary budget forecast prepared and presented to the School Board.
 • The Virginia Governor releases the proposed 2026-2028 Biennium Budget.
 • Based on the Superintendent and Cabinet review, the Budget and Financial Analytics Division
 prepares the SEON, which is the Superintendent’s Estimate of Needs to the School Board, for the
 future budget year.

January
 • The Superintendent presents the recommended budgets to the School Board at a public meeting.
 • The School Board holds numerous work sessions to review the Superintendent’s Estimate of Needs
 budget.

Expenditures are grouped into four main categories throughout the budget book: Personnel, Operations and
Maintenance, Capital Outlay and Transfers Out. Further subcategories and definitions are provided below.

PERSONNEL:
 Personnel & Fringe Costs: Salaries (both full-time equivalent employees and part-time such as
 substitutes), social security, retirement, group life insurance and health insurance are the major
 expenditures in this portion of the budget.
 For FY27, the Virginia Retirement System (VRS) rates changed as part of the state budget. The rates
 included in the FY27 Adopted Budget reflect the employer contributions as provided by VDOE and cover
 all Plan 1, Plan 2, and Hybrid employees.
 For plan year 2027, all employee, employer, and retiree premiums for Health, Dental and Vision
 Insurance will increase by 20%.

OPERATIONS AND MAINTENANCE:
 Contractual Services: The contractual services budget is used to pay outside contractors and other
 public entities or other school systems for services provided to LCPS. An example is the tuition paid to
 Fairfax County Public Schools for LCPS students to attend Thomas Jefferson High School for Science
 and Technology.

 Internal Services: The Self-Insurance Fund accounts for transactions associated with the comprehensive
 health benefits program, workers’ compensation insurance program, and the disability programs.

 Utilities and Communication: The utility and communication budget provides for the heating fuel,
 electricity, water, sewer and telephone services for 100 school buildings, 15 support buildings.

 Insurance: Insurance expenditures are for the property, casualty, liability, and fleet insurance carried by
 the school system.

 Materials, Supplies and Equipment: Expenditures include instructional supply allotments to each
 school, textbooks and minor instructional equipment such as computers, calculators, globes, maps, etc.

 Mileage Reimbursement: Mileage for itinerant teachers and other staff who travel on behalf of LCPS.

 Training and Continuing Education: Expenditures for training, workshops and conferences.

 Leases and Rentals: Lease or rental of heavy equipment needed for maintenance repairs.

CAPITAL OUTLAY:
 Capital Outlay: Major equipment purchases that cost in excess of $5,000; leases for buildings and land,
 and certain subscription-based information technology assets.

TRANSFERS OUT:
 Transfers out: Transfers from the LCPS funds to the Loudoun County government funds.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Grant Fund

The Grant Fund increases result from a combination of expected increases in local, state and federal grant
awards.

School Nutrition Fund

School Nutrition Services is a special revenue fund and should retain no more than 3 months of
expenditures in reserve. Student meal prices will remain flat for FY27.

Lease Purchase Fund

The Lease Purchase Fund remains at a flat $10 million per year funding for capital technology and fleet
purchases. For FY27, $7.2 million is designated for technology and $2.8 million for fleet vehicles and
equipment.

Self-Insurance Fund

The FY27 budget is predominantly comprised of claim expenditures that are projected to increase.
Revenues from health insurance premiums will increase due to a 20% rate increase for calendar year 2027
and improving rebate programs.

Capital Improvement Projects (CIP) Fund

The Capital Improvement Projects Fund has funding for VIEW Transition Academy, Visual & Performing
Arts Improvements for Middle and High Schools, Fleet Replacement, Technical Security Improvements,
CTAE Renovations for Middle and High Schools, Unified Communication System, Replacement of Non-
Inclusive Playgrounds and Tennis Court Lighting, High School, and other capital renewals and alterations.

Capital Asset Preservation Program (CAPP) Fund

The Capital Asset Preservation Program Fund will increase by $5.1m for capital maintenance repairs and
replacements.

Note: Loudoun County Public Schools are not permitted to incur long-term debt which includes debt
incurred for school division purposes. The county government is responsible for the issuance and
maintenance of debt for the school division.

adult education, self-funded summer school, and health services. The total amount is divided by the student
enrollment as of September 30 to determine an average per pupil cost for the current fiscal year and adopted
enrollment for the next fiscal year.
